message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for North Carolina Avenue.

I have $726 and a full pink monopoly with 4 houses each. I am mortgaged two properties and hold one get-out-of-jail card. Player 1 has a dangerous dark blue monopoly and only $29 cash. Player 3 is bankrupt.

Player 4 is in jail with $763 and a light blue monopoly. The auction for North Carolina Avenue is at $55, requiring a $56 minimum bid. I will cap my bid near $150 to mortgage the property and block Player 4 from completing a Pennsylvania Avenue plus North Carolina Avenue pair.

I should not jump past the $150 cap. If Player 4 bids higher, I will drop out and let them bleed. North Carolina Avenue cannot complete a green monopoly by itself; Pacific Avenue is mortgaged by Player 1 and Pennsylvania Avenue is mortgaged by Player 4.

Player 1 is nearly broke and could go bankrupt soon. If Player 4 wins North Carolina Avenue, they would own two greens and could potentially acquire Pacific Avenue from Player 1.

I am currently on Player 4's mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue, so I pay no rent. The real danger is Player 1's dark blue monopoly: Park Place with three houses and Boardwalk with four houses both carry very high rent.

Boardwalk with four houses charges $1700. Selling all twelve pink houses returns only $600, so I would need to mortgage St. Charles, States, and Virginia for roughly $220 to cover it.

I will continue bidding incrementally toward the $150 cap. Player 4 is in jail with $763 and matching every bid to acquire North Carolina Avenue.

Player 4's light blue set with four houses charges roughly $450 each. I can cover that from cash. I am checking exact pink house rent values.

Exact pink house rent values are now confirmed. I will raise to $56 and continue bleeding Player 4's cash toward the $150 cap.

Bidding $56 and mortgaging immediately nets $94 profit. At $149 the net is $1. The break-even point is $150, which costs $165 to unmortgage.

A two-green set would be devastating. North Carolina Avenue with four houses charges $1100 and a hotel $1275, while Pacific Avenue carries even higher rent. Player 1 is mortgaged on Pacific and nearly broke, so bankruptcy could auction those properties. I need to verify the exact bankruptcy rules.

Bankruptcy rules are now clear. A player who goes bankrupt to another player transfers all properties, while bankruptcy to the bank triggers an auction.

Player 1 is extremely vulnerable. Landing on my pink monopoly with four houses would bankrupt them instantly, and I would inherit Pacific Avenue, Park Place, and Boardwalk. If Player 4 also went bankrupt to me, I would acquire Pennsylvania Avenue as well.

This makes winning North Carolina Avenue even more critical. It would not only block Player 4 from completing a two-green set, but it would also give me a direct path to a full green monopoly.
